formulas.name: Area of a rectangle

variables.name: width
variables.description: The side at right angles to the length.

formulas.explanation: A rectangle of length l and width w can be tiled by l rows of w unit squares, so its area is l times w. Area units are squared length units, such as m² or cm².
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for floors, walls, screens, fields and any other rectangular surface.
assumptions: both lengths in the same unit

example.story: A bedroom floor measures 4.5 m by 3.2 m. How much carpet is needed?

formulas.name: Perimeter of a rectangle

variables.name: perimeter
variables.description: The total distance around the rectangle.

variables.name: width
variables.description: The side at right angles to the length.

formulas.explanation: Walking round a rectangle you pass each of the two lengths and each of the two widths once. Adding them gives 2l + 2w = 2(l + w).
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for fencing, framing, skirting boards or any distance around a rectangular shape.

example.story: A rectangular garden 6 m long is enclosed by 20 m of fence. How wide is it?

formulas.name: Area of a square
formulas.explanation: A square is a rectangle with four equal sides, so its area is side times side. This is where the word squared comes from. Going backwards, the side is the square root of the area.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for square tiles, plots and boards, or to find the side of a square with a known area.
assumptions: all sides equal and all angles right angles

example.story: A square patio has an area of 49 m². How long is each side?

formulas.name: Area of a triangle

variables.name: base
variables.description: Any side chosen as the base.

variables.name: height
variables.description: The perpendicular distance from the base to the opposite corner.

formulas.explanation: Two copies of any triangle fit together into a parallelogram with the same base and height, whose area is b times h. So one triangle has half of that. The height must be measured at right angles to the base, not along a sloping side.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it whenever you know a base and the perpendicular height of a triangle.
assumptions: the height is perpendicular to the chosen base

example.story: A triangular sail has a base of 3 m and a height of 5 m. What is its area?

formulas.name: Heron's formula
formulas.equation: A = sqrt((a + b + c)*(-a + b + c)*(a - b + c)*(a + b - c)) / 4
formulas.explanation: Heron's formula gives the area of a triangle from its three sides alone, with no angles or heights needed. With the semi-perimeter s = (a + b + c)/2 it reads √(s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)); the version in the equation is the same thing with s written out. It can be derived from the cosine rule and A = ½ ab sin C.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it when you know all three side lengths, for example for a plot of land measured with a tape.
assumptions: the sides satisfy the triangle inequality (each side shorter than the other two together)

example.story: A triangular field has sides of 13 m, 14 m and 15 m. What is its area?

formulas.name: Area of a parallelogram

variables.name: base
variables.description: Length of one side, taken as the base.

variables.name: perpendicular height
variables.description: Distance between the base and the opposite side, measured at right angles.

formulas.explanation: Cut a right-angled triangle off one end of a parallelogram and slide it to the other end: you get a rectangle with the same base and height. So the area is base times perpendicular height, not base times the slanted side.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for parallelograms, rhombuses and slanted shapes where you know the perpendicular height.
assumptions: h is measured perpendicular to b

example.story: A parallelogram has a base of 8 m and a perpendicular height of 5 m. Find its area.

formulas.name: Area of a trapezium (trapezoid)

variables.name: first parallel side
variables.description: One of the two parallel sides.

variables.name: height
variables.description: The perpendicular distance between the parallel sides.

formulas.explanation: A trapezium (called a trapezoid in American English) has one pair of parallel sides. Two copies, one turned upside down, form a parallelogram with base a + b and height h. One copy is half of that: the average of the parallel sides times the height.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for shapes with two parallel edges, such as cross-sections of ditches, roofs and ramps, and in the trapezium rule for integration.

example.story: A trapezium has parallel sides of 6 m and 10 m that are 4 m apart. Find its area.

formulas.name: Area of a rhombus or kite from its diagonals
formulas.explanation: The diagonals of a rhombus or a kite cross at right angles. The shape fits exactly inside a rectangle of size d₁ by d₂ and fills half of it, so its area is half the product of the diagonals.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for rhombuses, kites and squares when the diagonals are easier to measure than the height.

example.story: A kite has diagonals of 0.6 m and 0.8 m. How much fabric covers it?

formulas.name: Area of a circle

variables.name: radius
variables.description: Distance from the centre to the edge (half the diameter).

formulas.explanation: Cut a circle into many thin slices and lay them alternately point up and point down: they form a shape close to a rectangle with height r and width half the circumference, πr. The area is therefore πr times r. Doubling the radius makes the area four times larger.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for any round surface: pizzas, pipes, wheels, ponds, cross-sections of wires.
assumptions: use the radius, not the diameter

example.story: A pizza has a radius of 15 cm (0.15 m). What is its area?

formulas.name: Circumference of a circle

variables.name: radius
variables.description: Distance from the centre to the edge.

formulas.explanation: π is defined as the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter, so C = π × diameter = 2πr. For every circle, the distance around is a little more than three times the distance across.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to find how far a wheel rolls in one turn, the length of a circular track, or the edge of a round table.

example.story: A bicycle wheel has a radius of 0.35 m. How far does the bike travel in one full turn?

formulas.name: Arc length (radians)

variables.name: arc length
variables.description: Length of the curved part of the circle.

variables.name: angle
variables.description: Angle at the centre, in radians.

formulas.explanation: A radian is defined so that an angle of 1 radian cuts off an arc equal to the radius. An angle of θ radians therefore cuts off θ radius lengths. A full turn is 2π radians, which gives the whole circumference 2πr.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it whenever the angle is in radians: arcs, bends in roads, pendulum paths, angular motion.

example.story: A circular path has radius 2 m. How long is the arc for a centre angle of 1.2 rad?

formulas.name: Area of a sector (radians)

variables.name: sector area
variables.description: Area of the pie-slice shaped region.

variables.name: angle
variables.description: Angle at the centre, in radians.

formulas.explanation: A sector with angle θ is the fraction θ/(2π) of the whole circle. Multiplying that fraction by πr² gives ½r²θ. It looks like a triangle with base equal to the arc rθ and height r.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for pie slices, fan-shaped areas and the area swept by a wiper or a clock hand, with the angle in radians.

example.story: Find the area of a sector of radius 3 m with a centre angle of π/3 (60 degrees).

formulas.name: Arc length (degrees)

variables.name: angle
variables.description: Angle at the centre, in degrees.

formulas.explanation: An arc with centre angle θ degrees is the fraction θ/360 of the full circle. Multiply that fraction by the circumference 2πr to get its length.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it when the angle is given in degrees, as is usual at school.

example.story: Find the length of a 60 degree arc on a circle of radius 6 m.

formulas.name: Area of a sector (degrees)

variables.name: sector area
variables.description: Area of the pie-slice shaped region.

variables.name: angle
variables.description: Angle at the centre, in degrees.

formulas.explanation: A sector with angle θ degrees is θ/360 of the whole circle, so its area is that fraction of πr². A quarter circle, for example, has θ = 90.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for slices of round things when the angle is in degrees.

example.story: A quarter-circle flower bed has radius 4 m. What is its area?

formulas.name: Area of an ellipse
formulas.explanation: An ellipse is a circle stretched by different amounts in two directions. Stretching a unit circle by a in one direction and b in the other multiplies its area π by a times b. When a = b = r this is the circle formula πr².
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for oval tables, running tracks, planetary orbits and elliptical windows.

example.story: An oval rug has semi-axes of 5 m and 3 m. What is its area?

formulas.name: Perimeter of an ellipse (Ramanujan approximation)
formulas.explanation: Surprisingly, the perimeter of an ellipse has no simple exact formula; it needs an elliptic integral. Ramanujan found this approximation in 1914, and it is extremely accurate: for moderate shapes the error is far below one part in a million. For a circle (a = b) it gives exactly 2πr.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it whenever you need the distance around an ellipse, such as edging an oval table or the length of an elliptical track.
assumptions: approximation, accuracy decreases slowly for very flat ellipses

example.story: Estimate the edge length of an elliptical table with semi-axes 5 m and 3 m.

formulas.name: Area of a regular polygon

variables.name: number of sides
variables.description: How many equal sides the polygon has (3 or more).

formulas.explanation: A regular polygon splits into n identical isosceles triangles meeting at the centre. Each has base s and height s/(2 tan(π/n)), the apothem. Adding the n triangle areas gives the formula.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for hexagonal tiles, octagonal tables, stop signs and other shapes with equal sides and equal angles.
assumptions: all sides and all angles are equal
the angle π/n is in radians

example.story: A hexagonal paving tile has sides of 2 m. What is its area?

formulas.name: Sum of the interior angles of a polygon

variables.name: angle sum
variables.description: The total of all interior angles.

variables.name: number of sides
variables.description: How many sides the polygon has (3 or more).

formulas.explanation: From one corner you can draw diagonals that split any n-sided polygon into n - 2 triangles. Each triangle has angles adding to 180 degrees, so all the interior angles together add to (n - 2) × 180 degrees.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to find a missing angle in a polygon, or to check angle measurements.

example.story: What do the interior angles of a heptagon (7 sides) add up to?

formulas.name: Interior angle of a regular polygon

variables.name: interior angle
variables.description: Each angle inside the regular polygon.

variables.name: number of sides
variables.description: How many equal sides the polygon has.

formulas.explanation: In a regular polygon all n interior angles are equal, so each is the angle sum (n - 2) × 180 divided by n. Equivalently, each exterior angle is 360/n and the interior angle is 180 minus that.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for tiling questions, for example to see which regular polygons fit together around a point.
assumptions: regular polygon (all sides and angles equal)

example.story: What is each interior angle of a regular octagon, like a stop sign?

formulas.name: Volume of a cube
formulas.explanation: A cube with edge a holds a layers of a by a unit cubes, so its volume is a × a × a. This is where cubed comes from. Doubling the edge makes the volume eight times larger.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for boxes, dice and blocks with all edges equal.

example.story: A storage cube has edges of 30 cm (0.3 m). What is its volume?

formulas.name: Surface area of a cube

variables.name: surface area
variables.description: Total area of the six faces.

formulas.explanation: A cube has six identical square faces, each of area a². Adding them gives 6a².
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to find how much material wraps or paints a cube.

example.story: A gift box shaped like a cube needs 0.54 m² of wrapping paper to cover it exactly. How long is each edge?

formulas.name: Volume of a cuboid
formulas.explanation: A cuboid (rectangular box) is h layers of a rectangle with area l × w. So its volume is length times width times height. Remember that 1 m³ is 1000 litres.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for rooms, boxes, tanks, bricks and swimming pools with a flat bottom.

example.story: A garden planter is 2 m long, 1.5 m wide and 0.8 m tall. How much soil fills it?

formulas.name: Surface area of a cuboid

variables.name: surface area
variables.description: Total area of the six faces.

formulas.explanation: A cuboid has three pairs of identical opposite faces: top and bottom (l × w), front and back (l × h), and the two ends (w × h). Add one of each pair and double it.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for the amount of cardboard, paint or insulation needed to cover a box.

example.story: How much paint area does a 2 m by 1.5 m by 0.8 m wooden chest have on all six faces?

formulas.name: Space diagonal of a cuboid

variables.name: space diagonal
variables.description: Distance between opposite corners through the inside.

formulas.explanation: Use Pythagoras twice. The diagonal of the base is √(l² + w²); that diagonal and the height form another right-angled triangle whose hypotenuse is the space diagonal. Putting them together gives √(l² + w² + h²).
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to see whether a long object fits in a box, or for 3D distances.

example.story: What is the longest rod that fits inside a box 3 m by 4 m by 12 m?

formulas.name: Volume of a prism

variables.name: cross-section area
variables.description: Area of the end face (the shape that is repeated).

variables.name: length
variables.description: Distance between the two end faces.

formulas.explanation: A prism has the same cross-section all along its length, like a loaf of sliced bread. Its volume is that cross-section area times the length. Cuboids and cylinders are special cases.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for any solid with a constant cross-section: tents, beams, channels, packaging.

example.story: A tent is a triangular prism with a 6 m² triangular end and a length of 4 m. What volume of air does it hold?

formulas.name: Volume of a cylinder
formulas.explanation: A cylinder is a prism with a circular cross-section. Its volume is the circle area πr² times the height.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for cans, pipes, tanks, glasses and columns.

example.story: A drinks can has a radius of 3.3 cm and a height of 11.5 cm. What is its volume in m³?

formulas.name: Surface area of a cylinder
formulas.displayLatex: A = 2\pi r(r + h) = 2\pi r^2 + 2\pi r h

variables.name: surface area
variables.description: Two circular ends plus the curved side.

formulas.explanation: Unroll the curved side and it becomes a rectangle of width 2πr (the circumference) and height h. Add the two circular ends, each πr², to get 2πr² + 2πrh.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for the metal in a can, the label area plus lids, or the heat loss surface of a tank.
assumptions: closed cylinder with both ends; drop 2πr² for an open tube

example.story: How much aluminium sheet makes a closed can of radius 3.3 cm and height 11.5 cm?

formulas.name: Volume of a cone

variables.name: height
variables.description: Perpendicular height from base to tip.

formulas.explanation: A cone holds exactly one third of the cylinder with the same base and height, which you can check by pouring water. The same factor of one third applies to every pyramid, and calculus proves it by adding up thin circular slices.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for ice cream cones, funnels, piles of sand and conical roofs.
assumptions: h is the perpendicular height, not the slant height

example.story: An ice cream cone has a radius of 2.5 cm and a height of 10 cm. What volume does it hold?

formulas.name: Surface area of a cone
formulas.displayLatex: A = \pi r(r + l) = \pi r^2 + \pi r l

variables.name: slant height
variables.description: Distance from the tip to the edge of the base, along the surface.

formulas.explanation: The curved surface unrolls into a sector of a circle with radius l and arc length 2πr; its area is πrl. Add the circular base πr² for a closed cone.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for party hats, lampshades, conical tents and roofs.
assumptions: drop πr² if the base is open

example.story: A closed cone has base radius 3 m and slant height 5 m. Find its total surface area.

formulas.name: Slant height of a cone

variables.name: slant height
variables.description: Distance from tip to base edge along the surface.

formulas.explanation: The radius, the height and the slant height form a right-angled triangle inside the cone, with the slant height as hypotenuse. Pythagoras gives l from r and h.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to convert between perpendicular and slant height before using the cone area or volume formulas.

example.story: A cone has radius 3 m and height 4 m. What is its slant height?

formulas.name: Volume of a sphere

variables.name: radius
variables.description: Distance from the centre to the surface.

formulas.explanation: Archimedes showed that a sphere has two thirds of the volume of the smallest cylinder around it (radius r, height 2r, volume 2πr³). That gives (4/3)πr³. Volume grows with the cube of the radius.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for balls, bubbles, planets, droplets and spherical tanks.

example.story: A football has a radius of 11 cm. How much air is inside?

formulas.name: Surface area of a sphere
formulas.explanation: The surface of a sphere has exactly four times the area of a circle with the same radius. Archimedes found this by comparing the sphere with the curved side of a surrounding cylinder, which has the same area 2πr × 2r.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for paint on a ball, the area of a planet, or the surface a star radiates from.

example.story: Treating the Earth as a sphere of radius 6371 km, what is its surface area?

formulas.name: Volume of a pyramid

variables.name: base area
variables.description: Area of the base, of any shape.

variables.name: height
variables.description: Perpendicular height from base to apex.

formulas.explanation: Any pyramid or cone has one third of the volume of the prism with the same base and height. Three square pyramids with a common apex fit together exactly into a cube, which shows the factor 1/3 in one case.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for pyramids with square, rectangular, triangular or any other base.

example.story: The Great Pyramid of Giza originally had a square base of side 230.3 m (area 53 038.09 m²) and a height of 146.6 m. Estimate its volume.

formulas.name: Surface area of a square pyramid

variables.name: slant height
variables.description: Height of each triangular face, from the middle of a base edge to the apex.

formulas.explanation: The base is a square of area s². Each of the four triangular faces has base s and height l, so together they add 4 × ½ s l = 2 s l.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for the material needed for a square pyramid, such as a roof or a model.
assumptions: regular square pyramid (apex above the centre)

example.story: A square pyramid has a 4 m base side and a slant height of 5 m. Find its total surface area.

formulas.name: Volume of a frustum of a cone

variables.name: height
variables.description: Perpendicular distance between the two circular faces.

variables.name: large radius
variables.description: Radius of the larger circular face.

variables.name: small radius
variables.description: Radius of the smaller circular face.

formulas.explanation: A frustum is a cone with its top cut off parallel to the base, like a bucket or a lampshade. Its volume is the big cone minus the small cone that was removed, which simplifies to this formula. If r = 0 it becomes the cone formula, and if r = R the cylinder formula.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for buckets, flower pots, cups and cooling towers.

example.story: A bucket is 30 cm deep with a top radius of 15 cm and a bottom radius of 10 cm. How much does it hold?

formulas.name: Volume of a torus

variables.name: major radius
variables.description: Distance from the centre of the hole to the centre of the tube.

formulas.explanation: A torus (doughnut shape) is made by sweeping a circle of radius r around a circle of radius R. Pappus' theorem says the volume equals the circle's area πr² times the distance its centre travels, 2πR.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for rings, inner tubes, O-rings and doughnuts.
assumptions: r < R (the ring has a hole)

example.story: An inflatable swim ring has R = 10 cm and a tube radius r = 3 cm. What volume of air does it hold?

formulas.name: Surface area of a torus

variables.name: major radius
variables.description: Distance from the centre of the hole to the centre of the tube.

formulas.explanation: By Pappus' theorem, the surface swept by a circle of circumference 2πr moving around a path of length 2πR has area 2πr × 2πR. It is the same as the curved surface of a cylinder of radius r and length 2πR.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for the material in rings and tubes bent into a circle.

example.story: How much plastic skin covers a swim ring with R = 10 cm and r = 3 cm?

formulas.name: Volume of an ellipsoid

variables.name: first semi-axis
variables.description: Half the length along the first axis.

variables.name: second semi-axis
variables.description: Half the length along the second axis.

variables.name: third semi-axis
variables.description: Half the length along the third axis.

formulas.explanation: An ellipsoid is a sphere stretched by different factors along three perpendicular axes. Stretching multiplies volume by each factor, so the sphere's (4/3)πr³ becomes (4/3)πabc. With a = b = c = r it is the sphere formula.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for eggs, rugby balls, melons and the shape of the Earth.

example.story: An ellipsoid has semi-axes of 3 m, 2 m and 1 m. What is its volume?

formulas.name: Volume of a spherical cap

variables.name: cap height
variables.description: Height of the cap, from its flat face to the top.

variables.name: sphere radius
variables.description: Radius of the sphere the cap is cut from.

formulas.explanation: A spherical cap is the piece cut off a sphere by a flat plane, like the top of a dome. Adding up thin circular slices with calculus gives this formula. With h = 2r it gives the whole sphere, and with h = r a hemisphere.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for domes, lenses, the liquid in a partly filled round flask, and bowls.

example.story: A dome is a cap of height 2 m cut from a sphere of radius 5 m. What volume does it enclose?
